subject: Abnormally high abundance and density estimates

messages.author: 293d911d5114407e
messages.subject: Abnormally high abundance and density estimates
parts:
Hi everyone! im working on analyzing distance sampling data conducted on two study sites in northern kenya. All species observed were recorded, however I am only interested in giraffe. I seemed to have fit the detection function pretty well (see attached) however my density and abundance estimates are very high, and i'm not sure what is causing it. Below is my code, any help would be greatly appreciated!

giraffe<-data[data$Species=="Giraffe",]
head(giraffe)

region2<-read.csv("region.csv",stringsAsFactors = F)
samples2<-read.csv("samples.csv", stringsAsFactors = F)
obs2<-read.csv("obs.csv",stringsAsFactors = F)

ds.dht.model <- ds(giraffe,.25,region.table=region2,sample.table=samples2,obs.table=obs2)
summary(ds.dht.model)
plot(ds.dht.model)
gof_ds(ds.dht.model)

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Abnormally high abundance and density estimates
parts:
Nicole

Not able to troubleshoot your problem completely as although you've included 3 of your data files, you've not included the file used to create the "data" object.

One of the inconsistencies in what you have provided is a discrepancy between the "obs.csv" contents and what is shown in your summary statistics.  When I perform a quick summary on your "obs.csv" file, I find

> table(xx$Region.Label, xx$Sample.Label)
          
            0  1  2  3  4  5  6  9
  Loisaba   9  0  2  2  1  3  3  1
  Namunyak 25  2  1  0  0  0  0  0

This shows 28 detections in the Namunyak stratum and 21 detections in the Loisaba stratum.  However, the summary you provided shows 27 detections in Namunyak and 86 detections in Loisaba.

You might start there to check your data.  If you don't track down your problem, perhaps send along the file responsible for the "data" object.

messages.author: 9dce01a6123da978
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Abnormally high abundance and density estimates
parts:
Hi there,

As Erik said, it's hard to be sure exactly what the problem is with the data you've supplied, but having looked at the output I can't help thinking that units might be part of the issue. Your abundance estimate for the two study areas is 5.5m. I just had a quick look on the internet and found that a recent global estimate for wild populations of giraffe is 97,000. You haven't given units anywhere here, but I imagine that for an animal the size of a giraffe, the X axis of your detection should be in km? I'm just wondering if Distance thinks your distances are specified in metres? If you divide your densities and abundances by 1000000 (to convert from per metre squared to per km squared) then you get approx 55 giraffes over the two areas. Does that sound more sensible?

Best wishes,

Mark

messages.author: 293d911d5114407e
messages.subject: Re: Abnormally high abundance and density estimates
parts: I wanted to post to inform everyone the solution to my issues. The first issue stemmed from the set up of the data collection. I learned that it is essential to record transects that are driven, even if no animal is seen. This is represented and taken into account in the analysis by listing the number of visits to each transect, and then multiplying that number by the transect length. I also learned the importance of making sure all units are uniform across the board. One of my issues stemmed from having my transect length in meters and distance was in km. In addition, even once all the data was reformatted, my estimates were still  high with high standard error, probably because the number of detections (25) is very small. The suggested number of detections (Buckland et al. 2001) needed to produce credible density estimates is 60-80 observations. Also, our transects were driven rather than walked at one of our locations, which causes potential bias due to the fact that roads are inherently not random.
